title: Powell says student loan system at top of her in-tray
description: Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education se
body: Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education secretary.Labour's deputy leader told the BBC she stood by comments she made in February that the interest rates graduates with Plan 2 loans were paying were "egregious".She said she was committed to looking at the issue, although acknowledged she "can't make any promises" about changes.Plan 2 loans were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.In November last year, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the repayment threshold for students with Plan 2 loans would be frozen at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of rising with inflation.The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.Campaigners have called for that decision to be reversed.Reeves later said the government's measures were "fair and proportionate" for getting "the balance right between tax and spending".In April, the government said interest on some student loans in England - including Plan 2 - would be capped at 6%.Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, Powell said she was "very familiar" with the issue as her eldest child has a Plan 2 loan.She said: "I think it's not just about the threshold of when people start to pay it back, but also the interest rate which is RPI [retail prices index] plus 3%."I think I've called it in the past egregious and I'm not going to change my opinion on that just because I'm now the secretary of state."The government has committed to a review of that, it's very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state, and I want to make sure we look at this so it's fair for students."Powell described it as a "real cost-of-living issue" for young people, adding: "They're paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan."Pressed on whether it is something she will look at, Powell replied: "Yes. I can't make any promises, but it needs looking at."MPs on the Treasury Committee this month said comparing student loan repayments to phone contracts or cinema tickets "amounted to mis-selling" by government.It came after a BBC investigation found the government compared student loan repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.Earlier this year, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would cut the rate of interest charged on Plan 2 loans, capping it at RPI only. The current RPI rate is 3%.

schema.headline: Powell says student loan system at top of her in-tray

title: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'
description: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptationImage source, Universal PicturesByEmma SaundersCulture reporterUpdated 2 hours agoSi
body: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptationImage source, Universal PicturesByEmma SaundersCulture reporterUpdated 2 hours agoSir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy.Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie.Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky.""The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, Lupita Nyong'o stars as Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey"It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth," Wilson wrote, while also acknowledging that Sir Christopher's work had sparked renewed interest in Homer's classic."The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves... [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments."Nolan... is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful."Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, The Odyssey is Sir Christopher Nolan's first film since the Oscar-winning OppenheimerBut she was left largely disappointed by the three-hour epic"I had hoped that Nolan's affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters," she wrote."But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality... the film's vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants."Wilson added that her teenagers had "had a good time" seeing the blockbuster at the cinema."It's a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display - and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth," she said."There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material. But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem."During his press tour for the film, Sir Christopher told Empire magazine, external that he used the opening line of Wilson's translation ("Tell me about a complicated man") as a guide for his Odysseus, played by Matt Damon.Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, Anne Hathaway plays Odysseus's wife Penelope, who's also mother to their son Telemachus (Tom Holland)In contrast to Wilson's take, the latest adaptation has received rapturous reviews from film critics.It is the director's first movie since 2023's Oppenheimer, which won the Academy Award for best picture.The Telegraph declared The Odyssey the "film of the year", while Metro added that the movie would "change cinema forever".The Times described it as "a masterpiece in every way", and the Standard praised the film as a "colossal piece of cinema".The Odyssey, which was released earlier this month, stars Zendaya, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, Charlize Theron alongside Nyong'o and Damon.It follows Odysseus (Damon), the Greek king of Ithaca, on his long and perilous journey home from the Trojan War to return to his wife and son (Hathaway and Holland).

schema.headline: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'

title: House of the Dragon star Bethany Antonia joins Strictly Come Dancing 2026 line-up
description: House of the Dragon star Bethany Antonia is the latest celebrity to join this year's line-up for Strictly Come Dancing.Antonia has portrayed dragon-ri
body: House of the Dragon star Bethany Antonia is the latest celebrity to join this year's line-up for Strictly Come Dancing.Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.In a statement, Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"She is the ninth celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including  Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer and Jaime Winstone.More celebrities are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up.Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition. The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me"."I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year. Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair."I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You."I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.  Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show. "I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers."I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

schema.headline: House of the Dragon star Bethany Antonia joins Strictly Come Dancing 2026 line-up

title: Robert Bush: Legacy funeral boss 'left baby's remains on floor for two years'
description: Kadie Laws, whose father Darren Laws' ashes were recovered from Legacy, sobbed while reading her statement.She recalled shouting "it better not be my
body: Kadie Laws, whose father Darren Laws' ashes were recovered from Legacy, sobbed while reading her statement.She recalled shouting "it better not be my dad in there" when she first heard about the police investigation.Laws, who suffers from PTSD, depression and anxiety following the loss of her father, said she felt "extreme anger" towards Bush. "My family and I are never going to heal from this trauma. I'll never be myself again and that's because of Robert Bush."Kerry Webb also became emotional as she told the court how her mother, Julie Webb, was one of the bodies found by police.Instead of being cremated, her mother had been left in the parlour and it took police seven weeks to identify her, she said."How could someone be so cruel? Seven weeks of heartbreak, of not knowing if it was truly my mum inside that coffin, of not knowing what had happened to her body, of being terrified that somebody had hurt her."Bush's fraudulent activity was laid out to the court, detailing how he gave 46 families the wrong ashes and 11 were given nothing at all.Prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said the total monetary value of the fraud was £86,868 and that Bush had conned 226 people who paid him for funeral plans, pocketing more than £550,000 over an 11-year period.  Among the victims was Shelley Chearman, who lost her husband Alan.She told Bush: "You fooled a lot of people in Hull with your mild manner, when in fact you are a cruel conman. You use people's grief to fund your lifestyle."Outlining the case on Monday, Paxton told the court bodies had been discovered "on the racks" of a cold storage area and one was found on a stretcher on the floor.The vast majority were "uncovered and in varying states of decomposition" and the  funeral home was "dirty and unkempt".The 48-year-old's crimes were discovered by chance while he was on holiday, after two funeral directors tipped off police.Bush, of Otley, West Yorkshire, was arrested when he landed at Heathrow Airport days later and told police he had debts of about £90,000, Paxton said.The hearing continues.Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.

schema.headline: Robert Bush: Legacy funeral boss 'left baby's remains on floor for two years'

title: How afraid should we be of Scotland's jellyfish?
description: Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in ScotlandByClaire ThomsonBBC ScotlandWh
body: Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in ScotlandByClaire ThomsonBBC ScotlandWhen scuba diver and underwater photographer Ross McLaren encountered a jellyfish for the first time, he said all he felt was "sheer terror". "I was diving in the Clyde and one of the instructors had to pull me out of the way of the tentacles as it was wafting above me," he said. McLaren ended up with a sting across his upper lip but said it did not stop him from wanting to dive.Many people are scared of jellyfish due to the fear of painful stings and the creature's unpredictable nature in the water.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Scuba diver Ross McLaren has completed almost 600 dives since 2016But McLaren, who lives near the coast in North Ayrshire, believes there is more to the brainless, heartless and boneless invertebrates than people might think. "Jellyfish have such a bad reputation but they are one of the most mesmerising and beautiful creatures underwater," he said, having completed almost 600 dives.As we reach peak jellyfish season in Scotland, should we see them as a sight to behold or a reason to run?When do you see the most jellyfish in Scotland?July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in Scotland."The number and distribution of jellyfish are impacted by many different factors," said Anna Bunney of the Marine Conservation Society, which runs a nationwide survey of jellyfish."This includes sea temperatures, the availability of plankton for feeding, which peaks during the summer months when it is warmer, and ocean currents."Sea temperatures tend to lag behind air temperatures, Bunney says.The maximum air temperatures in Scotland usually occur in July and August, whereas sea temperatures are at the warmest in August and September.When the sea starts to get warmer, it means a return of the jellyfish.Image source, James LynottImage caption, Sea temperatures, the availability of plankton, and ocean currents have an impact on jellyfish sightings in ScotlandBunney described jellyfish as weak swimmers or "passive drifters" which rely on ocean currents to carry them. Calmer ocean conditions around the UK in the summer months help to push jellyfish gently towards the shore, meaning there are often more sightings of the creatures.Breeding speed also increases with warmer conditions, allowing adult jellyfish to reproduce in large numbers, creating so-called blooms.These blooms can look like a thick soup or pulsing cloud in the water and have been known to block boat engines. In 2011, Torness nuclear power station in East Lothian was even shut down as a precautionary measure due to huge numbers of jellyfish found in sea water entering the plant.Image source, Marc KilpatrickImage caption, A bloom of moon jellyfish washed up on Seafield Beach in Kirkcaldy, Fife, in JulyMcLaren added that while jellyfish season is normally April to October, the creatures can still be seen in Scotland's waters all year round."You see them in the winter months but they are far more prevalent and common during the summer," he said.What happens if a jellyfish stings you?Jellyfish stings in Scotland are not usually life-threatening but can be very painful.Depending on the type of jellyfish, the stingers may not be sharp enough or long enough to pierce the skin.Bunney said most jellyfish have stinging cells but the severity and detectability of the sting varies widely between species.Swimmers should be aware of the Lion's Mane, which is a brownish orange colour, and prevalent around Scotland's coastline in the warmer summer months. They have long tentacles which can give a sore but not lethal sting.The tentacles can break off and float around in the sea or become attached to chains on a boat, for example, but the stinging cells will stay alive even when not attached to the main body.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, The Lion's Mane jellyfish have long tentacles which can give painful stingsBunney, who said she has been stung a lot by jellyfish, compared a mild sting to that of a nettle."There was one point when every time over a period of two years I was stung by a jellyfish when I was out in the sea," she said."But thankfully, it hasn't impacted how I feel about the ocean."In fact, what I often think is the most frustrating is when you are stung but you cannot see what you have been stung by."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, The Barrel jellyfish has eight arms and is not normally harmful to humansMcLaren said he has never been put off scuba diving by the prospect of a jellyfish sting but he can understand why swimmers might be nervous."When you're diving, as long as the visibility is good, you can negotiate your way around a jellyfish relatively easily, if you know what way the current is flowing and you pay attention," he said. "Swimming, on the other hand, I totally get it - if I was taking my kids down to the beach and there were a lot of jellyfish I would probably stop them from getting in the water."When you're swimming you tend to have your head out of the water more so you can't always see what is underneath or know where the tentacles are going."Both Bunney and McLaren added that it is important not to touch a jellyfish when it is washed up on a beach as it can still sting, even when presumed dead.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Jellyfish tentacles can still sting when not attached to the main bodyBunney said to follow NHS guidance after a jellyfish sting.It suggests using tweezers or the edge of a bank card to remove the tentacles as soon as possible as they can continue to sting while attached to the body.A heat pack or immersion in hot water can reduce pain and swelling, and painkillers such as paracetamol can also help. If symptoms because more severe or a sensitive part of body has been stung, seek medical help. Why do jellyfish sting?Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Jellyfish sting as an automatic reflex, not a deliberate attackUnlike bees or wasps, which sting as a defence mechanism to protect themselves, a jellyfish sting is an automatic reflex, not a deliberate attack."A common misconception is jellyfish go after people but contact with a jellyfish is actually merely incidental and humans are not on their menu," Bunney said."They are not actively stinging, it is just when anything touches their tentacles as they are moving through the water, regardless of what it is."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Small fish often live among jellyfish tentacles for protectionJellyfish tentacles are lined with thousands of venom-filled stinging cells. When touched, these cells fire toxic harpoon-like tubes designed to paralyse prey, such as plankton and small fish.Should jellyfish stop you from swimming in the sea?"Do not be afraid but be cautious" is the advice from Bunney, who generally recommends swimming calmly away from jellyfish."Most of the species found in Scotland have very mild stings, which only cause minor irritation, and some are completely harmless," she said.Bunney says it is important for people to learn about the different species of jellyfish and report sightings to the Marine Conservation Society."People think jellyfish are ugly," she said. "But they are really beautiful creatures that come in all different colours and sizes."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Bunney said most species found in Scotland only have mild stingsMcLaren echoed the love for the marine invertebrate. "People hate jellyfish but I always do my best to take a photo of one when I see it because they are impressive to see in the water," he said."It's almost like stars in the night sky when you are on the sea floor and looking up at the jellyfish above you."It's magical."

schema.headline: How afraid should we be of Scotland's jellyfish?

title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral in Guildford
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Penelope Keith (pictured in 1980) was an actressByZac Sherratt and Joshua AskewSouth EastUpdated 1 hour
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Penelope Keith (pictured in 1980) was an actressByZac Sherratt and Joshua AskewSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoDame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress"."It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service."It caught her completely. She was very special."Image caption, Many people gathered to pay their respects to the late actressBrandreth described Dame Penelope as one of the nicest and kindest people. "Her love of Surrey was in everything she did," he said. "Her sense of community... belonging and working for the community was considerable."Image caption, Dame Penelope was described as "great fun"Sarah Cliff told BBC Radio Surrey Dame Penelope had been part of her childhood. "[She] was known to me as Auntie Penny", said Cliff. "She was great fun". Cliff, the daughter of the acting couple Michael Robbins and Hal Dyer, added that the service was "beautiful". "I've never been to this cathedral. It's airy, it's light, it's lovely," she said. Image caption, Sarah Cliff (pictured) is the daughter of actors Michael Robbins and Hal DyerDoreen Walford said she and the late actress went back a long way. She told BBC Radio Surrey the pair used to live close by and they had worked together. "Everybody could talk to her," she said.On seeing the procession, she added: "I am so glad I came. It was absolutely amazing." Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk , externalor WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Booker Prize longlist 2026: Elizabeth Strout and Douglas Stuart among 13 authors recognised
description: Elizabeth Strout, Douglas Stuart, Marlon James and Rebecca Perry are among the authors who have been longlisted for this year's Booker Prize. The 13 c
body: Elizabeth Strout, Douglas Stuart, Marlon James and Rebecca Perry are among the authors who have been longlisted for this year's Booker Prize. The 13 chosen books include novels set in Mexico City, a remote Scottish island, an assissted suicide clinic in Zurich, 1980s Jamaica, post-apocalyptic Kent, and coastal Massachussetts before the 2024 US election.Chair of the judges Mary Beard described the 13 novels as "dynamite", adding: "We are confident that our longlist of books has something for everyone."The longlist, referred to as the Booker Dozen, will be whittled down to a shortlist on 22 September, before the winner is announced on 9 November.The annual Booker Prize is the literary world's most prestigious award, recognising long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the UK or Ireland.The six shortlisted authors will receive £2,500 each and a specially bound edition of their book, while the eventual winner will receive a trophy and £50,000 in prize money. High-profile authors who missed this year's longlist include Maggie O'Farrell, Ann Patchett, John Lanchester, Deborah Levy and Julian Barnes, who many predicted would be recognised for his final book Departure(s).Three of this year's authors in the Booker Dozen are previous shortlistees, including Elizabeth Strout, who is recognised for The Things We Never Say.It follows a high school history teacher in Massachusetts who is grappling with isolation, post-pandemic social anxiety, and concern about the forthcoming 2024 US election.The two other former shortlistees have also previously won the prize. Shuggie Bain author Douglas Stuart is recognised this time for John of John, about a young gay man who returns to his strict religious family on a remote Scottish island.Another former winner, Marlon James, returns this year with The Disappearers, a 600-page book due to be released in September about eight gay men in Kingston, Jamaica, who are targeted by a violent mob during a play rehearsal.James's is the longest book this year, while the shortest is Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman - a 140-page novel which follows a disgraced professor touring an idyllic countryside house, learning about its previous owner. Another longlistee, Rebecca Perry, won the Waterstones Debut Fiction Prize earlier this month for her novel May We Feed The King, about a curator of historic buildings who begins to explore the life of an almost-forgotten medieval king. Two other authors are recognised for debut works - including Kenan Orhan for The Renovation, about a psychologist caring for her dementia-suffering father in Italy when some building work doesn't go to plan.Fellow debut novelist Djamel White is recognised for All Them Dogs, which follows a man returning to west Dublin after being on the run for five years because he killed someone in a gang fight.Aged 28, White is the youngest longlistee this year. The oldest is 81-year-old M John Harrison, for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in a Kent coastal town.Switzy by Emma Cline, due to be published in September, is about a wealthy and accomplished man travelling to an assisted suicide clinic in Switzerland; while The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis sees an encounter in a Mexico City hospital lead to a life-changing friendship.Gwendoline Riley's The Palm House, meanwhile, follows a London freelancer and her long friendship with a senior magazine editor; and Missouri Williams's The Vivisectors follows a graduate student in a decaying university city overrun by wild plants.The list is completed by Luke Kennard's Black Bag, about a penniless out-of-work actor who is paid to zip himself inside a large black leather bag and sit silently at the back of a university lecture hall for a psychological experiment.

schema.headline: Booker Prize longlist 2026: Elizabeth Strout and Douglas Stuart among 13 authors recognised

title: Naga Munchetty swaps BBC One's Breakfast for Radio 5 Live Breakfast
description: Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about £360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.She
body: Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about £360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct. That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

schema.headline: Naga Munchetty swaps BBC One's Breakfast for Radio 5 Live Breakfast

title: Wildfires in south-west France flare up as region braces for new 40C heatwave
description: This summer's fourth heatwave was expected to start by Wednesday, bringing temperatures in the area to 40C.Similar temperatures are expected in Spain.
body: This summer's fourth heatwave was expected to start by Wednesday, bringing temperatures in the area to 40C.Similar temperatures are expected in Spain.Dozens of communities are still threatened by wildfires that forced more than 70,000 to evacuate their homes over the last week - although many have now been allowed back.The Madrid region has been especially affected, but Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said while there were highly challenging hours and days ahead, light was beginning to appear "at the end of the tunnel".In neighbouring Portugal, 400 firefighters were tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area.The French city of Bordeaux, which has a population of 260,000, is not currently under threat, according to officials, despite the fact that one of the wildfires burning on Monday came only 15km (9 miles) from the city's periphery. But Commander Rémi Lassoureille, who is leading the firefighting response in the Gironde region, is still worried about the western edge of the wildfire."We are frightened about the impact on Bordeaux and the metropolitan area," he said. Air quality in the city also deteriorated greatly."By Sunday evening everything had really begun to empty out," a holidaymaker from Essex told the BBC, adding that the air was "really smoky" with bits of ash. "People were staying indoors, so it was eerie, and very sad."The majority of residents and tourists were wearing masks and the smell of smoke clung on to clothes for days, she said. A firefighter "got a round of applause" as he walked through the Marché des Chartrons in Bordeaux where restaurants were having to close their doors because of the ash in the air, she added."The city has been very quiet," said Graham White, president of the Bordeaux British Community. "The shops, restaurants and cafes are fairly empty... Interestingly on Sunday when there was still smoke, there were people brave enough to sit outside on terraces."White, who has been living in the area for several years, said this sort of event was "something significant". But some news reports had suggested the situation in Bordeaux was "akin to being the next Great Fire of London", which was not the case, White added.Health Minister Stéphanie Rist said the government was being "very vigilant" in terms of air pollution and urged people in the affected areas to stay indoors. On Tuesday morning the Gironde prefect ordered a new evacuation of all camping sites near the coast at Lacanau, while those in the nearby town were allowed to stay put but told to prepare for sudden evacuation. About 4,000 tourists told to leave the area are in addition to the 220,000 people evacuated around France in recent days. An estimated 240 homes and houses have been destroyed, officials have said.By midday on Tuesday firefighters were already intervening in various parts of the region to tackle fires that were picking up again. A 23-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of starting a fire in the Var region. is now facing 15 years' imprisonment. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 184 people had been arrested since 6 July in connection with the fires.Peggy Plouhinec, the general director of Château Picque Caillou - one of the few wine estates on the west side of Bordeaux - told the BBC that her business chose to close at the weekend because of the smoke, but that the situation had improved since then and that a bout of rain on Sunday night had helped. While her vineyards were not at risk, she said tourists had "deserted" the region. "The hospitality sector will be impacted this summer, that's for sure," she added. "What is happening is unprecedented. We're lucky that we haven't been too affected yet, but the business will still suffer from the lower numbers of tourists.""But many people have lost their homes or their businesses, not to mention the firefighters who have been hard at work for weeks now and who must be exhausted."One resident of Cap Ferret, which was evacuated late last week, told French media that his main concern now was for the peninsula he lived in, rather than the big city city inland."Everyone talks about saving Bordeaux, but in Bordeaux there's nothing but concrete. Have you ever seen concrete burn?""Here, there are only trees... and when you see all that has burned, it's a catastrophe."Additional reporting by Xavier Pallas

schema.headline: Wildfires in south-west France flare up as region braces for new 40C heatwave

title: World Cup: Uefa furious at reports Fifa plan to sell stakes in tournament
description: European football's governing body Uefa has reacted furiously to proposals from Fifa to seek private investment in its competitions, including the Wor
body: European football's governing body Uefa has reacted furiously to proposals from Fifa to seek private investment in its competitions, including the World Cup.Fifa - the sport's global governing body - said it intends to expand "football development funding" to more than $10bn (£7.5bn) and invite third-party investment in a new venture.The story was first reported in the Financial Times and the Times, with the latter claiming the plans could potentially earn Fifa president Gianni Infantino tens of millions of pounds.In a lengthy statement outlining the proposals, Fifa says it will " invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to "consolidate" its commercial and event operations.Fifa say that once approval has been granted, Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.Fifa sources have told BBC Sport there has been no discussion over Infantino, or anyone else, becoming chief executive of the new body.In its statement, Fifa did say Infantino and the rest of the organisation "has a duty" to control the development of the project.Fifa has not said precisely what that means, or what the specific nature of Infantino's involvement will be.As part of its pitch Fifa says all member associations will be able to access up to $20m (£15m) in "one-off capital" to fund development.Infantino said every nation should benefit from the riches football creates."Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value - and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game," he said."Our job is to make sure the rest of football grows with it: Fifa exists to support sustainable, inclusive development in every corner of the world."However, Uefa has issued a statement criticising the proposals, which it claimed "crosses a line".Fifa argues its plan, with a dedicated commercial subsidiary, is similar to that used by governing bodies in other sports.In 2018, Premiership Rugby announced a partnership with private equity and investment advisory firm CVC Capital Partners.However, Uefa sees Tuesday's announcement as a step too far - and raises the potential for further expansion of Fifa competitions in order to raise revenue, both in terms of size and frequency, which could threaten its own lucrative competitions."This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," Uefa said."Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder who cares about the future of the game."The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa's to sell."Fifa says it would retain control of FFE "and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, the international match calendar and all regulatory and sporting decisions".The matter is likely to be a topic of conversation at the next Fifa Council meeting in the autumn and then around the Fifa Intercontinental Cup, featuring Champions League winners Paris St-Germain, in December.The proposal could be voted on by all 211 members at the Fifa Congress in Morocco in March.

schema.headline: World Cup: Uefa furious at reports Fifa plan to sell stakes in tournament

title: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks
description: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on hu
body: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on human rights to that of authoritarian states.The diplomatic row was initially sparked last week, when the US joined North Korea and Russia in voting against extending Volker Turk's term as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. After the vote on Friday, France's UN mission criticised the US and compared it to North Korea and Russia. "The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore," it posted on X, external.In response, US ambassador Mike Waltz accused France of voting for a human rights chief who had been "lecturing" democratic countries while "cozying up to the world's worst oppressors", without elaborating on what he meant.Turk has criticised Russia's war in Ukraine and Israel's military conduct in Gaza.The US team's walkout came while France's ambassador Jerome Bonnafont was speaking during an emergency Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.US ambassador Dan Negrea said the delegation would continue to make similar protests until France "renounces their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric".The fight over Turk's second term, which was passed with 144 states in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions, reflects tensions between Washington and the United Nations.The Trump administration has cut funding for UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of its entities.On Friday, US ambassador Jeff Bartos criticised Turk's reappointment and said "there will be consequences" to the assembly which "tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts". "The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding," he said.However, French ambassador Bonnafont described Turk as "a voice of conscience" who demonstrated "rigor and impartiality" during his first term.Deputy UN spokesperson Farhan Haq declined to comment on the US walkout, adding the UN expected all member states to respect the decision.

schema.headline: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks

title: Is it safe to travel to France and Spain right now?
description: Figure caption, Travelling to France or Spain? What you need to know as wildfires continueByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 3 hours agoWildfir
body: Figure caption, Travelling to France or Spain? What you need to know as wildfires continueByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 3 hours agoWildfires in Spain and France have caused mass evacuation and disruption, with more than 300,000 people forced to leave their homes and many sleeping in sports halls and other temporary shelters.An official from one of the French departments affected by the fires has pleaded with visitors to stay away.On Sunday, Sophie Brocas, prefect of the French department of Gironde, said, "I urge tourists not to come," while advising those already there to consider an alternative destination.For those who have upcoming holidays to the affected regions, here is what you should know about how it might impact your plans.Should I travel to France or Spain right now?The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment". "You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.To know if this applies to you, check your policy.Where are the wildfires burning?The UK government says parts of Gironde and Landes in the south west of France are affected.As of Tuesday, the official French wildfire map gives Gironde the highest fire alert level. Meanwhile, Var has its second highest alert level.The map says there are more than a dozen fires burning across the country, including on Corsica.More than 42,000 hectares of land has been burnt in Gironde and some 240 homes have been destroyed.In Spain, authorities have declared a national emergency because of wildfires in parts of Madrid and Ávila. The UK government says there are also reports of wildfires in other inland areas of Spain.Does travel insurance cover wildfires?Once again, the answer depends on your policy."If your travel plans are disrupted by a wildfire and your policy includes trip disruption cover then travel insurance may cover some of the resulting costs," says Chris Bose, director of general insurance policy at the Association of British Insurers (ABI).However, only half of travel insurance policies have "catastrophe" cover, according to analysis from Defaqto.This means that, in many cases, travellers might not be covered by their insurance in the case of wildfires.To know if this does or does not apply to you, speak to your insurer or check the wording of your policy.What should I do if my airline or accommodation cancels my booking?In the case of cancelled flights or accommodation, Bose recommends seeking refunds from your airline, tour operator or accommodation provider in the first instance.Duthie says if your airline cancels your flight due to wildfires then "they should offer you the chance to rebook, or provide a full refund".She says if your holiday was booked as a package then this refund should cover "all elements", including flights, accommodation and transfers. "But if you've booked everything separately, you'll need to deal with each provider independently. Your airline may refund your flight, but your accommodation provider may not if the property is unaffected."Should I just cancel my trip now?Check what your insurance policy says about flights, accommodation or trip bookings first.Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel, says this is especially true for those not due to travel in the next week or two."Travellers who cancel now will likely forfeit their right to a refund or rebooking," he says.As the UK government has not warned against travel to anywhere in the two countries, he says travellers are "unlikely to be able to claim on their travel insurance"."As a rule, insurance firms won't make allowances for 'disinclination to travel'," Boland says."Instead, holidaymakers should wait until closer to the departure date to see if the holiday can go ahead or what flexible booking options are offered from the tour operator or airline. "Travel companies will be prioritising anyone due to depart in the next couple of days."How will climate change affect travel insurance in the future?The amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe has increased by 57% since summer 2022, according to the World Health Organization.It adds that climate change is intensifying wildfires and increasing their frequency.Duthie says insurance firms are adapting to "potential new and increasing risks involved in travel as a result".In the near term, she says it is unlikely insurance providers will change their policies."Current clauses may refer to 'severe' or 'extreme' weather, but the definitions for these can vary and currently no providers go as far as to specify criteria such as maximum temperatures."However, she says that "longer term there is a chance that we may end up seeing less insurable destinations and increased premiums".Get in touchAre you affected by issues discussed in this story?  Do you have any questions?

title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' in English Channel mid BBC interview
description: Figure caption, A French Navy boat was heard firing shots during a BBC interview earlierByDaniel SextonSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoA French Navy patro
body: Figure caption, A French Navy boat was heard firing shots during a BBC interview earlierByDaniel SextonSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoA French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises."It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."Image source, BBC/Jack ValpyImage caption, Chris Philp MP, the Shadow Home Secretary, said it felt like an intimidation tactic or warning shotsThe captain of the fishing boat which hosted the interview, Matt Coker, said he had "never seen anything like it before".The French authorities said the boat, PSP Flamant, was not engaged in an operation to monitor migrant boats.Keohan said there were 17 shots, adding: "There was no warning for our boat, no signs given that this was the French's intention."Philp said it "felt to me like an attempted intimidation to stop us covering migrant crossings".Image source, Richard Pohle/The TimesImage caption, A French patrol officer at the back of the boat was seen pointing a pistol towards the seaAt sea, Keohan described it as "the most unusual moment... in the quiet of the Channel" when the gunshots rang out mid-interview.A French patrol officer at the back of the boat was seen pointing a pistol towards the sea. It is believed that is where the shots came from.Keohan, who was on board the vessel with a reporter from The Times, added: "There was no warning for our boat, no signs given, that this was the French's intention. "Even now it's still not clear what the patrol boat was aiming at."Image source, Chris Philp MPImage caption, The MP was being interviewed by the BBC at the time of the incidentAfter the incident, Philp said: "It is extraordinary that the French Navy will fire live rounds to defend their waters against a visiting British politician but cannot bear to do anything about stopping illegal Channel crossings."If France showed people smugglers half the seriousness they showed me, the boats would stop. "Instead, the French wave them through and pass them off to the British coastguard so it's our problem."He said he would be raising the issue with the French ambassador.'Normal activity'A UK government spokesperson said: "This is a matter for the French authorities."The French authorities said a handgun shooting exercise had taken place by the public service patrol boat Flamant off the coast of Cap de Gris-Nez.A spokesperson said: "In order to maintain their high level of operability in the current international context, the units of the French Navy train regularly."Individual training of the combatant is part of the normal activity of a ship in operations."The regulatory signals as provided for by international standards for this shooting exercise were displayed, and the safety gauge was respected."This exercise is unrelated to the presence of a British ship in the area, which was out of range of fire."The PSP Flamant was not engaged in an operation to monitor migrant boats."Earlier this month, a Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 46 miles (74km) south of Plymouth.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Roberto Mancini next Italy manager after Andrea Pirlo controversy
description: Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both approached by the FIGC about the Italy job before Pirlo.Mancini, 61, previously managed Italy from 2018 un
body: Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both approached by the FIGC about the Italy job before Pirlo.Mancini, 61, previously managed Italy from 2018 until 2023 and won Euro 2020 - beating England in the final at Wembley.He led the Azzurri to a world record 37-game unbeaten run, but failed to qualify for the 2022 World Cup - losing to North Macedonia in a play-off - and resigned in August 2023.Another World Cup play-off failure for Italy earlier this year meant they were absent from this summer's tournament and spelled the end of Gattuso's tenure, with his contract terminated in April by mutual consent.Despite their big stage successes, Italy have not featured at a World Cup finals since 2014.Under-21 manager Silvio Baldini had taken over on a temporary basis following Gattuso's departure.Former Italy and Sampdoria midfielder Mancini led Manchester City to their first Premier League title in 2012 and enjoyed success with Lazio and Inter Milan, winning the Coppa Italia with both and three Serie A titles with Inter.He also spent time with Galatasaray and Zenit St Petersburg before taking on the Italy job in 2018.After he departed from the Azzurri, he had a short spell with the Saudi Arabia national team before joining Qatari side Al Sadd.Although they won the Qatar Stars League, they failed to reach the final four of the AFC Champions League Elite and lost in the Qatar Cup final. Mancini left his role with Al Sadd in June.Italy start their Nations League campaign on 25 September at home to Belgium before travelling to face Turkey three days later.

schema.headline: Roberto Mancini next Italy manager after Andrea Pirlo controversy

title: Saltburn Cricket Club: 'Finger-clicking' cheating claim in Saltburn-Norton match investigated
description: An amateur cricket match has made global headlines after a fielder was accused of cheating by clicking his fingers to get a wicket.The North Yorkshire
body: An amateur cricket match has made global headlines after a fielder was accused of cheating by clicking his fingers to get a wicket.The North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League has started an investigation into a second XI Division 2 game between Saltburn and Norton.A viral video on social media appears to show a Saltburn fielder clicking his fingers as the ball passes Noman Shabir's bat before being caught by wicketkeeper Josh Bowes. Saltburn appeal and the umpire gives Shabir out.It has been suggested that the finger-clicking was designed to trick the umpire into thinking the batter edged the ball.Saltburn won by 159 runs and are top of Division 2 by 18 points."The league have received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday," the league said in a statement on X."A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made."Last week Bowes took eight catches in Saltburn's 22-run win over Shildon Railway. The men's Test record for catches by a keeper in an innings is seven.Bowes leads the league standings with 31 catches, 10 more than any other player.Rory Cotterill, who captained Middlesbrough second XI during a 29-run defeat by Saltburn last month, responded to a social media post containing the video and alleged two further incidents of cheating by Saltburn in that match.The original video of the incident has had more than five million views on X, with publications in Australia and New Zealand among those to report it.BBC Sport understands a meeting between Saltburn, the league and legal representatives is due to take place on Tuesday night. Norton declined to comment.

schema.headline: Saltburn Cricket Club: 'Finger-clicking' cheating claim in Saltburn-Norton match investigated
